To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

fecal indicator organism (FIO) release to surface waters during baseflow periods is due to hyporheic flow between sediment pore water to the overlying water and that the FIO release rates are higher than the previously estimated rates.

(a) FIO concentrations in a slug of surface water increase during transit through a reach during baseflow conditions; (b) this increase is likely due to hyporheic flux of FIOs from the stream bed; and (c) the magnitude of the increase is a function of the magnitude of the flux.

(a) concentrations of fecal indicator organisms (FIs) were significantly higher in water column at the outlet of stream reach compared to the inlet in baseflow conditions, indicating that the bottom sediment was a source of FIs, (b) the rate of release of FIs from bottom sediment was higher in baseflow conditions compared to storm flow conditions, and (c) no diurnal trends were seen in the release rates of FIs from the bottom sediment.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the fate and transport of E. coli and Enterococcus bacteria in stream reaches.
the enrichment of stream water with FIOs in baseflow conditions.
the fate of E. coli and Enterococcus spp. in streams during baseflow conditions and the potential for these organisms to be transported from bottom sediment to the stream water column.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the hyporheic zone is a source of FIOS to the overlying water during baseflow conditions.
FIOs are present in surface waters not only due to direct deposition or through transport in surface runoff but also due to release from bottom sediments through hyporheis exchange.

FIOs in surface waters are not always due solely to direct fecal deposition or through transport in surface runoff but also through hyporheis exchange between sediment pore waters and the overlying stream water column during baseflows.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
FIO release rates to stream water during baseflow periods are higher than previously thought and that FIO release rate is independent of time of day.
FIOs in surface water are a function of hyporheic flux, sediment pore water concentration of FIOs, and the sediment hydraulic conductivity.

FIOs are enriched during baseflow period through hyporheisic exchange and that this enrichment is a function of the FIOs concentration in sediment pore water and not the concentration of the conservative tracer.
The main takeaway from our work is that

FIO concentrations can increase in the same volume (slug) of water during baseflow conditions, and this phenomenon is likely due to release of FIOs from sediment pore water into the stream water column.
the mass balance-based method is a viable approach to estimate net rate of release of FIOs into the surface water during the baseflow.
FIO release rates from the bottom sediment are not negligible and can be significant during the baseflow periods.
